client: I've been really dreading this networking event I have to go to next week for work. Every time I think about it, my heart starts racing and I get this sick feeling in my stomach — just the idea of walking up to strangers and introducing myself makes me want to cancel the whole thing. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like even just thinking about this event brings up a lot of anxiety — that racing heart and sick feeling are your body's way of signaling that this feels really threatening to you. I also notice that you came here despite part of you doubting it will help, and I think that took some courage. What is it about walking up to strangers that feels most overwhelming — is it more about what they might think of you, or something else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think it's mostly about what they'll think of me — like, I'll say something awkward or boring and they'll just kind of look for an excuse to walk away. And then I'll be standing there alone, which honestly feels worse than not going at all. It's like I'm already convinced it's going to go badly before I even walk through the door.
therapist: What you're describing is a really common but painful thinking pattern — your mind is essentially writing the whole story before it's even happened, and casting yourself as the one who fails. That prediction of rejection feels so real that it's already shaping how you feel *now*, which is exhausting. I'm curious — can you think of a time in the past where you expected a social situation to go badly, and it actually turned out differently than you feared?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... maybe. There was a work dinner a few months ago where I was dreading it the whole week before, and it actually ended up being fine — I talked to a couple people and it wasn't a disaster or anything. But I don't know, this feels different somehow, like that was a smaller group and I already knew a few people there, so I'm not sure it really counts.
therapist: It's really interesting that you found that example almost immediately, and then quickly moved to explain why it doesn't count — I wonder if that's your anxiety's way of protecting its own story, because if that success *does* count, it starts to challenge the prediction that things always go badly for you. That dinner sounds like genuine evidence that you can hold your own socially, even when you were dreading it beforehand. What do you think would happen to the anxiety if you let yourself give that experience a little more credit?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess if I actually let myself believe that dinner was a real win, maybe the anxiety wouldn't have quite as much to stand on — like, I couldn't say "I always mess these things up" if I have proof that I don't. But it's hard to hold onto that because the fear still feels so loud and convincing in the moment, you know? It's like I know logically that it went okay, but emotionally it just doesn't stick the same way the bad predictions do.
therapist: You've just articulated something really important — that gap between *knowing* something and *feeling* it is at the heart of what makes anxiety so stubborn, and you're definitely not alone in experiencing that. The good news is that's actually something we can work on directly, because the brain learns more from repeated experience than from logic alone. I'm wondering — when you imagine arriving at that networking event next week, is there one small, concrete thing you could do that might give you another piece of evidence like that dinner, rather than trying to "conquer" the whole event at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess maybe I could just aim to have one real conversation with one person, instead of feeling like I have to work the whole room. But even saying that out loud, I'm already thinking about what happens if that one conversation goes badly — like, then I've failed my only goal and it'll feel even worse than having no goal at all. I don't know if setting a small target actually takes the pressure off or just makes it more concentrated.
therapist: You're thinking about this really carefully, and I notice there's something worth gently flipping here — the goal of "one real conversation" isn't actually about *passing or failing*, it's about gathering information, just like that work dinner did. What if instead of framing it as a target you could fail, you thought of it as an experiment where any outcome — even an awkward one — tells you something useful? An awkward conversation that you survived is still evidence against the story that you can't handle these situations.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I like the idea of calling it an experiment — it does take some of the pass/fail pressure off, at least in theory. But I think my brain is going to have a hard time actually believing that in the moment, like when I'm standing there feeling awkward, I doubt I'll be thinking "oh great, useful data." I guess I'm just not sure how to hold onto that reframe when the anxiety is actually hitting me in real time.
therapist: That's such an honest and important point — reframes are easy in a calm moment and genuinely hard to access when your nervous system is in full alarm mode. One thing that can help is creating a kind of "anchor" ahead of time, like a single short phrase you decide on *now* that you can return to in the moment — something like "this is just data" or even "I've done this before." Would it feel worth trying to come up with something like that together, something simple enough that anxious-you might actually be able to grab onto it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think I'd be willing to try that — something short actually makes sense because I know I won't be able to remember a whole pep talk when I'm panicking. Maybe something like "I've gotten through this before" since it ties back to that dinner, which felt real. I just worry that even saying it to myself will feel hollow in the moment, like I won't actually believe it when I need to.
therapist: "I've gotten through this before" is actually a really strong choice because it's rooted in something real, not just a generic affirmation — and that specificity matters. The worry that it'll feel hollow is worth sitting with, because sometimes those phrases need to be *practiced* in low-stakes moments first, so they're already a little worn-in by the time you need them under pressure. What if you tried saying it to yourself a few times this week, even just when you're thinking about the event, so it starts to feel a bit more like yours?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I can try that, I guess — it feels a little strange to just repeat something to myself in the middle of the day, like I'll feel kind of silly doing it. But I think I see the logic, that if I've already said it a few times before the event it won't feel like I'm reaching for something completely foreign. I just hope it actually does something and isn't one of those things that sounds good in a therapy session but falls apart in real life.
therapist: The skepticism you're naming is actually healthy — it means you're not just taking this on blind faith, and that kind of critical thinking will serve you well. What I'd gently point out is that you've already done something like this today: you came in doubting it would help, and yet here you are having built something real and specific that's actually grounded in your own experience. That's not a therapy-session trick — that's you doing the work.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's... actually a fair point, and I didn't really think about it that way until you said it. I guess I did come in skeptical and something still came out of it, which is kind of hard to argue with. I think I'm still nervous about the event, but maybe slightly less convinced that it's going to be a complete disaster.
therapist: That shift — from "it's going to be a complete disaster" to "maybe not a complete disaster" — is actually more significant than it might sound, because it means you've loosened anxiety's grip on the story just a little, and that's real progress. I notice you said it in a way that still sounds a bit tentative, which makes sense — you don't have to be fully convinced right now, just open enough to show up and run the experiment. How are you feeling about the week ahead?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, which I wasn't expecting. I'm still dreading the event, but it's more like a manageable dread now rather than this wall I couldn't see past. I think the thing I'm most worried about is getting to Tuesday and having all of this fade, and just being back to that sick feeling with nothing to hold onto.
therapist: That image of "manageable dread instead of a wall" is a really meaningful shift, and I want you to hold onto that description because it came from you. The worry about Tuesday is understandable, but you're not walking into it empty-handed anymore — you have a real anchor phrase, a real piece of evidence from that dinner, and the experience of today showing that your skepticism doesn't have to stop you from making progress. Would it help to take just a moment before we finish to remind yourself of those three things, so they feel a little more solid going into the week?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
